World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Horticultural production losses reach $25 million after cyclone
World.content:
Fruit and vegetable producers in Western Australia's Gascoyne are estimated to have suffered losses above $25 million from Tropical Cyclone Narelle.

The category three system last month tore through the Gascoyne town of Carnarvon, 890 kilometres north of Perth, which produces fresh food for domestic and export markets valued at almost $1.5 billion a year.

A clearer picture of the extent of the damage has begun to emerge nearly one month after the event, with early results from a grower impact survey.

Phil Frzop says Carnarvon produce makes up 70–80 per cent of Perth's winter fresh fruit and vegetable market. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Carnarvon Growers Association (CGA) president Phil Frzop said the initial infrastructure damage and crop losses from Cyclone Narelle were "huge".

He expected the $25 million damage bill would rise in the coming months.

"It's going to have a big impact across the board through employment, and some growers probably might not even be able to continue," Mr Frzop said.

Damage widespread

Grower Tam Chinnery was expecting to harvest her crop of oranges shortly after Narelle passed, but the cyclone "smashed" her orchard with wind gusts of up to 133km/h.

"A lot of the fruit just dropped on the ground, and we'd already lost a bit of fruit from the previous cyclone," she said.

Tamara and Jeremy Chinnery estimate their damage bill to be between $100,000 and $180,000. (Supplied: Tamara Chinnery)

"What didn't drop on the ground was just absolutely bruised, scratched [or] pummelled."

Ms Chinnery said her farm was able to salvage some oranges and send them to Perth for juicing, but the poor fruit quality meant a significant price cut.

"No-one wants to buy an orange that's got big bruises and scars all over it," she said.

"It's costing us a lot of money to send it down on the odd hope that someone's going to buy it and use it for juice."

The cyclone caused extensive damage to the Chinnerys' crops. (Supplied: Tamara Chinnery)

Ms Chinnery said damaging winds from Narelle "sandblasted" her ground crops.

The flooding that came a few days after Cyclone Narelle's strong winds marked the fourth natural disaster to hit the region this year, after Cyclone Mitchell in February and a heatwave in January.

Farms in some areas along the Gascoyne River also suffered crop damage from the flooding.

More than 6 metres of water flowed through the Gascoyne River. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

Calls for more financial assistance

State government grants of up to $5,000 were made available to small businesses and primary producers impacted by Cyclone Narelle.

Mr Frzop said that amount "wouldn't do much" to help local farmers.

Banana crops were destroyed during Cyclone Narelle. (ABC News: Andrew Chounding)

"If you have a look at Queensland and areas like that, when they flooded last year, they were given about $70,000 per farm," he said.

"The region just wants to be supported and recognised for what it actually is because we seem to get left behind in the mineral boom.

" You can't eat iron ore. "

WA Agriculture Minister Jackie Jarvis, who visited the town this week, has not responded to multiple ABC interview requests.

World.title: White House seeks firing squad, electrocution, gas for federal executions
World.content:
US President Donald Trump's administration has announced it plans to add firing squads, electrocution and gas asphyxiation as alternative methods of executing people convicted of the gravest federal crimes, noting difficulties in obtaining drugs for lethal injections.

The recommendation came in a report from the Department of Justice, released on Friday, local time, on what it would take to fulfil Mr Trump's promise to resume capital punishment at the federal level in his second term, although it will likely be several years before another federal execution can be scheduled.

Shortly before his first term ended in 2021, Mr Trump, a Republican, resumed executions at the federal level after a 20-year gap, putting 13 federal prisoners to death with lethal injections in his final few months in office.

There had been just three federal executions in the preceding 50 years, with most executions in the US carried out by state governments.

Donald Trump approved the execution of 13 federal prisoners in his final months in office. (Reuters: Sarah Silbiger)

Returning to the White House last year, Mr Trump rescinded a moratorium on federal executions put in place by his predecessor, former president Joe Biden.

Mr Trump's Justice Department is now seeking the death penalty against more than 40 defendants across the country, although none have yet gone to trial, each of which can take years.

Acting Attorney-General Todd Blanche — the president's former criminal defence lawyer — wrote in his introduction to the 52-page report that the Biden administration's moratorium had "undermined the federal death penalty and left victims, their families, their communities, and the Nation to bear the consequences".

Old methods, plus a new one

In the report, Mr Blanche instructed the Justice Department's Bureau of Prisons to modify its execution protocol "to include additional, constitutional manners of execution that are currently provided for by the law of certain states", pointing to the older methods of firing squads and electrocution, and the new gas asphyxiation method pioneered by Alabama in 2024.

Adding alternative methods to the protocol will allow for executions "even if a specific drug is unavailable", the report said.

Todd Blanche has recommended the changes to the president. (Reuters: Elizabeth Frantz)

Mr Biden, a Democrat, commuted the sentences of 37 of the 40 men awaiting executions on federal death row, leaving only three behind: Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, convicted in 2015 for the deadly bombing of the Boston Marathon; Dylann Roof, convicted in 2017 of killing nine worshippers at a South Carolina church; and Robert Bowers, convicted in 2023 of killing 11 people at the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

The US is one of the very few Western nations that still uses the death penalty, although public support for capital punishment has gradually declined among Americans.

According to long-running Gallup surveys, 52 per cent said they supported it for murder last October, the lowest in more than 50 years, while 44 per cent said they opposed it.

Legal challenges remain daunting

It can take years for condemned prisoners to exhaust all legal avenues for challenging their death sentences, and none of the three men on federal death row is eligible, under current Justice Department rules, to be given execution dates.

Typically, when a US state or the federal government adopts a new execution protocol, death row prisoners can mount legal challenges arguing the new method violates the US Constitution's prohibition of "cruel and unusual punishments".

Report names 2022 the 'Year of the Botched Execution' More than one-third of all US execution attempts went wrong in 2022, as support for the death penalty continued to decline.

Such challenges have always failed at the US Supreme Court, which has never previously found an adopted execution method to be unconstitutional. However, some methods, including the firing squad and electrocution, have not been revisited by the court since the 19th century, and the court has not yet agreed to hear challenges to gas asphyxiation.

Lethal injection remains the most common method in the US, but has a higher rate of being botched than other methods, including the single-drug protocol adopted by the federal government in 2019 favouring the use of pentobarbital, a powerful barbiturate.

Some executions have been aborted as prison officials struggled to find a vein on a strapped-down prisoner. Opponents of the method say autopsies of executed people's lungs show they experienced torturous drowning before dying as a result of the drug.

Pharmaceutical companies also refuse to sell prison systems drugs that can be used in executions, partly to comply with a European Union ban.

US prisons have therefore had to seek out smaller, less-regulated compounding pharmacies willing to brew copies of those drugs.

This has led to several US states reviving older methods in recent years.

A man demonstrates in South Carolina in 2025, ahead of the firing squad execution of Brad Sigmon. (Reuters: Shannon Stapleton)

Five states have firing squads, with Idaho set to adopt it as its primary method in July, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit research group in Washington.

Last year, South Carolina carried out the first execution by firing squad in the US in 15 years.

In 2024, Alabama became the first state to execute someone by forcing nitrogen into their airways through a face mask, suffocating them. This method has since been adopted by Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi and Oklahoma.

'A stain on our history'

Some opponents of executions have now criticised Mr Trump for adopting these additional methods.

Cassandra Stubbs, director of the American Civil Liberties Union's Capital Punishment Project, said the Justice Department "embraces forms of execution that have been widely denounced for their cruelty and unnecessary infliction of extreme pain".

Senator Dick Durbin, the ranking member on the Senate's Judiciary Committee, criticised the Justice Department in a statement that called the death penalty barbaric and "a cruel, immoral, and often discriminatory form of punishment".

" State-sanctioned killing is not justice," he said. "These actions will be remembered as a stain on our nation's history. "

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Tiny mountain possum bred at lower altitudes due to climate change
World.content:
For the past six years, Trevor Evans has seen the number of endangered mountain pygmy possums at his sanctuary increase sixfold.

The pocket-sized possums are traditionally found on the peaks of the Snowy Mountains, but are being bred at a lower altitude at the Secret Creek Sanctuary in Lithgow in the NSW Central Tablelands to prepare them for the impacts of climate change.

"We started off with six possums many years ago," Mr Evans said.

" We've grown the population to about 36. Our work is instrumental [in its survival]. "

Trevor Evans says the mountain pygmy possum is facing extinction. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

Weighing less than 100 grams, the mountain pygmy possum is Australia's only hibernating marsupial, spending up to seven months of the year sleeping under the snow.

There are fewer than 2,000 individual possums living in the wild as a changing climate exposes them to growing threats.

"They are quite unique, very special, and disappearing," Mr Evans said.

" With the loss of snow in the Snowy Mountains, it allows predators to come up in the summer and feed on them. "

The possums spend seven months of the year hibernating under snow and rocks. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

Changing habitat

In collaboration with the University of NSW, the sanctuary is attempting to better prepare the species for living in warmer temperatures by breeding them at an altitude of 1,000 metres.

The species is usually found above 1,400 metres.

"Breeding them here at 1,000 metres will help them live through climate change," Mr Evans said.

"We are adapting them to lower altitudes, higher temperatures and different mating cycles.

" They have the opportunity to breed twice in a season. They breed quite readily if you give them the right opportunities. "

Mountain pygmy possums are found in the Snowy Mountains, but climate change is threatening their habitat. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

The idea to breed them at a lower altitude came after the discovery of a 25-million-year-old fossil belonging to a direct ancestor in the Riversleigh World Heritage Area, north of Mount Isa.

University of New South Wales biological sciences professor Michael Archer said it showed the species had not always lived in the Snowy Mountains.

"Every time we see this species in the fossil record, it is always in fossil communities that were cool temperate lowland rainforests, not alpine environments," Professor Archer said.

"Every signal to us says they are not in their comfort zone now; they're struggling to survive by the skin of their teeth.

"If we could get them back into their ancestral comfort zone, the lowland rainforest, we predict that they will be very happy."

Michael Archer says the mountain pygmy possum is more suited to living in lowland rainforests. (Supplied: UNSW)

The possums have become reliant on snow coverage, providing insulation for their nests under the rocks.

Professor Archer said they would be unable to survive in the alpine regions if snow coverage were reduced further by global warming.

"For these possums, that would be lethal," he said.

"If the snow disappears, the wintry cold winds will end up going down into these rock piles and kill the possums."

While the colony at Secret Creek Sanctuary will remain in captivity, Mr Evans hoped the population could be used to support efforts to increase numbers in the wild.

"To be able to breed some from the wild that are currently geographically isolated from each other is a goal," he said.

"We would like to breed those and then return those possums to the wild."

It is hoped that the possums that return to the Snowy Mountains will be more predator-aware and better able to deal with warmer temperatures.

Critical research

During hibernation, the species lives deep under snow and rocks, giving scientists little understanding of the animal's daily life for much of the year.

The population of mountain pygmy possums at the Secret Creek Sanctuary has grown from six to 36. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

Mr Evans said observing the marsupials in a controlled environment had been educational.

"We filmed them mating for the first time. We filmed the little nest that they make when they hibernate in winter," he said.

"We get a better understanding of what they're eating, how they're surviving, where they actually live, how they nest, and how they hibernate as well.

" If we understand them, we can help manage them. "

The Secret Creek Sanctuary in Lithgow is home to hundreds of native animals, including koalas. (ABC Central West: Hamish Cole)

The Secret Creek Sanctuary has been operating for more than 30 years and contains hundreds of native species, many of which are endangered.

For Mr Evans, protecting the mountain pygmy possum from extinction had become a critical part of the shelter.

"It feels really good to be involved," he said.

"If we don't do it, and no-one does, it's a species that we could lose.

"We need to [put in] an all-out effort, and the critical thing is funding and support."

World.title: Tears, hymns and prayer as thousands gather at Anzac services in Sydney
World.content:
During an early start on a crisp Saturday morning, thousands of people gathered at the Cenotaph in the heart of Sydney's CBD to commemorate Anzac Day.

At the Cenotaph in Martin Place — the monument commissioned to recognise Australian soldiers and sailors who served during World War I — 11,000 attendees listened to prayers and sung hymns dedicated to the fallen.

Chris Minns recited Elliott Napier's poem, Salute, before laying a wreath. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Attendees have gathered at the Cenotaph in Martin Place on Saturday. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The NSW Premier Chris Minns continued with a long-standing tradition and recited Elliott Napier's poem, Salute, before laying a wreath at the foot of the Cenotaph.

Other notable guests in attendance were Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane, City of Sydney Lord Mayor Clover Moore, Federal MP Tanya Plibersek on behalf of the prime minister, and state Governor Margaret Beazley.

The service marks 111 years since Gallipoli. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Wreaths were laid while tears where shed in an emotional service. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Among the crowd, some held wreaths adorned with the words "Lest We Forget" while others pinned sprigs of rosemary and rows of medals to their shirts.

The service was briefly disrupted just after 4:30am, when Indigenous pastor Uncle Ray Minniecon was met with boos during his Welcome to Country address.

Uncle Ray Minniecon at the dawn service in Sydney. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Loading...

The Indigenous pastor, who served for two years with the 51st Battalion, told the ABC he wanted the hecklers to understand "this always was and always will be Aboriginal land".

"They should show respect to us as Traditional Owners," he said.

Brigadier Vincent Williams described the booing as "the most appalling act". (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Brigadier Vincent Williams, acting president of RSL NSW, said it was "the most appalling act" he has ever seen at a dawn service.

"His [Uncle Ray] family have contributed enormously to this nation through the First World War to the current day.

The service ended with the Last Post, followed by a minute's silence. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

Thousands of attendees listened to prayer and sung hymns dedicated to the fallen soldiers. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

NSW Police confirmed a 24-year-old man was arrested and charged with commit nuisance on a war memorial.

He has been granted conditional bail to appear before Downing Centre Local Court on June 3.

In response to the booing, Mr Minns said Anzac Day "should always be treated with the respect, solemnity and reverence it deserves".

"Whilst I've never before heard booing like that at a dawn service, I've also never heard a crowd spontaneously applaud as they did for Uncle Ray Minniecon," he said.

The service ended with the Last Post, followed by a minute's silence, and the singing of the Australian and New Zealand anthems.

The service in Castle Hill attracted thousands of attendees. (ABC News: Tamsyn Buckle)

The local service, organised by the Castle Hill RSL, attracts more than 10,000 people every year. (ABC News: Tamsyn Buckle)

In Sydney's north-west, thousands gathered for the Castle Hill RSL service, which attracts about 10,000 people every year.

As part of the service, the lights at Centenary of Anzac Reserve were switched off in respect for the dozens of veterans who marched in.

As the sun rose, about 50 wreaths were laid by various local servicemen and women, as well as the family members of veterans to commemorate their Anzacs.

It was one of many local ceremonies that were held across the state this morning.

Marches and services to mark the 111 years since Gallipoli were held from Waverley Park in the eastern to suburbs, to Penrith in Western Sydney to Yass in the Southern Tablelands.

World.title: Scrapped anti-whaling ship bought for $10 makes conservation comeback
World.content:
The MV Steve Irwin spent more than a decade defending the world's oceans.

After more than seven years out of action, the former Sea Shepherd ship has been restored to its former glory and will return to marine conservation as Ship4Good.

Kerrie Goodall bought the ship for just $10. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

The flagship anti-whaling vessel was retired in 2019, bound for a junkyard in Hong Kong.

"It was going to be scrapped," Ship4Good founder and skipper Kerrie Goodall said.

Unable to bear the thought of losing "an important part" of Australia's maritime history, Ms Goodall bought the ship for just $10.

Since 2022, Ms Goodall and a crew of volunteers have been working to restore the ship and get it sea-ready.

Ship's 'claim to fame'

In its prime, the MV Steve Irwin fought anti-whaling campaigns in the Southern Ocean, ramming Japanese whaling ships and shutting down illegal Chinese drift netters.

"It was a war down there," Ms Goodall said.

Sea Shepherd claims the MV Steve Irwin helped save the lives of more than 6,000 whales during its 10-year tenure.

The vessel took part in 17 campaigns with conservation group Sea Shepherd. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

"Every year for 10 years, they went back to the Antarctic and protected the Australian Marine Sanctuary from illegal whaling," Ms Goodall said.

"That is the ship's claim to fame."

The ship's blue-and-grey camouflaged exterior has become synonymous with Newcastle Harbour, where it has docked since 2022.

The original plan was for the ship to become a floating museum and function space that could be used to educate the public on ocean conservation.

However, with the help of engineer and volunteer Steve Ward, the ship is ready to sail again.

The ship will depart Newcastle with touches of local art. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

Ms Goodall said she had spent about 4,000 hours working on the vessel, removing rust and restoring the ship's interior.

She even took on work for a local paint company to learn how to paint the ship.

"This is my legacy," she said.

" I've sold everything I have, businesses, properties, everything. "

Return to conservation

Having now left Newcastle Harbour, the ship will berth at Melbourne's Docklands, where it is primed for a return to maritime conservation.

For up to two months a year, the ship will work on collaborative marine campaigns along Australia's east coast.

Planned campaigns include the removal of marine debris and the reduction of invasive species.

"It's an eco battleship, and it deserves to be memorialised," Ms Goodall said.

When docked, the vessel will be open to the public for tours.

Ship4Good departs Newcastle harbour on its way to Melbourne. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

World.title: 'Generous gift': James Valentine's voluntary assisted dying legacy
World.content:
A master behind the microphone, James Valentine's legacy from effortlessly connecting with audiences to spotlighting jazz now extends to raising critical awareness of voluntary assisted dying (VAD).

The veteran 702 ABC Sydney broadcaster, 64, passed away at home using VAD two years after a cancer diagnosis.

For someone who revelled in finding joy in the ordinary and bringing humanity to radio, one of Valentine's final wishes was to make it publicly known his choice to access NSW's VAD laws.

In doing so, Valentine and his family further broke down the taboos associated with the subject, said colleague and friend Andrew Denton.

"To talk openly about voluntary assistance dying, it takes a bit more of the stigma away," he told 702 ABC Sydney.

"He had limited time, but because he knew he was in control of the end, his time was spent with his friends, with his family, and with love."

The beloved presenter hosted radio and television shows across the ABC for 30 years. (Supplied)

Denton credited Valentine for his vulnerability and emotional intelligence in the way he spoke of death.

In dying, James Valentine taught us how to live James helped us make sense of life and gave us permission to laugh at the absurdity of it all — and ourselves.

"So many people are traumatised by the very word 'death' and certainly the word 'cancer' that they shut down. And I think James modelled something very healthy," he said.

For Valentine's wife Joanne and their two children, Ruby and Roy, they said they felt grateful he was "given the option to go out on his own terms".

"In his final moments, he was still concerned about making a difference and that was something that was so important to him," Ruby told 702 ABC Sydney.

" He wanted it to be something that people knew that he did, that … he could lend his voice to the argument of why this is such a necessary thing for so many people. "

'People need to know about it'

VAD in Australia is heavily safeguarded and governed by some of the strictest laws in the world.

Queensland and NSW now account for almost two-thirds of all assisted deaths in Australia.

The Northern Territory is the only jurisdiction in Australia where VAD remains illegal. A commitment has been made, however, by the territory government to draft and debate VAD legislation in 2026.

Denton founded national charity Go Gentle Australia, which provides information and education on end-of-life choices.

Andrew Denton has spoken fondly of James Valentine and his lasting legacy. (AAP: David Mariuz)

Their 2026 State of VAD report highlighted key barriers to access for eligible people, such as process complexity and difficulties in finding trained practitioners in regional and rural locations.

Research from Queensland University of Technology in 2025 found only 62 per cent of Queensland health practitioners surveyed correctly identified that VAD was legal in their state.

Go Gentle Australia CEO Linda Swan said education remained critical.

"We clearly have strong evidence now that the voluntary assisted dying laws that have been legal in Australia for over six years are delivering safe, careful, compassionate care," Dr Swan said.

"People need to know about it."

Linda Swan urged Australians to have a conversation with their families, carers and health professionals about end of life choices. (Supplied)

Federal roadblock remains, says advocate

In NSW in particular, there are VAD care pathways in place across all 15 local health districts and a centralised navigation service, Dying with Dignity NSW president Penny Hackett said.

An issue across the country, however, is the federal restrictions of electronic communication in the VAD process.

The Criminal Code Act made it an offence to use a carriage service to publish or distribute material that counsels or incites a person to suicide.

A technicality, in theory, means no conversations about the delivery or administration of a VAD substance can therefore take place over the phone, video call or email between a practitioner and patient.

Experts and Australian suicide prevention organisations agree VAD should not be described as suicide because conflating the two can be damaging.

"The ban on telehealth for voluntary assisted dying consultations causes an access issue in regional areas," Ms Hackett said.

"We have been pushing for years to try and get it overturned."

Penny Hackett says advocates believe the ban on telehealth for voluntary assisted dying must change. (AAP: Joel Carrett )

Ms Hackett said many end-of-life care advocates were grateful to Valentine and his family for their "generous gift" in opening up the conversation.

"People just don't want to talk about death and dying," she said.

"For people generally, VAD or no VAD, the more openly you can express your wishes, the better your end of life is going to be.

"The generous gift that James and his family have given us is a really significant moment in terms of getting those discussions going."

Dr Swan added: "I'm sure he and his family were very proud of the impact he had.

World.title: Why Australia's weather map has ground to a halt
World.content:
No, the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) website is not glitching, Australia's weather map has ground to a halt.

Seven-day forecasts from Darwin to Melbourne, and everywhere in between, reveal a monotonous similarity — for some towns, a variation of less than 1 degree Celsius through the entire week.

The stagnant pattern is due to a stationary "blocking high" in the Tasman Sea, and there is no sign the system will break down at any point in the foreseeable future.

This is not BOM data error, the Brisbane forecast is the same every day during the next week: showers and 25C or 26C. (ABC News)

Groundhog day extends to a fortnight

In the mid-latitudes, highs and lows ordinarily move steadily east (due to Earth's rotation), and a typical system takes only three or four days to cross Australia.

However, occasionally the atmosphere over a region becomes immobile thanks to the presence of a "blocking high", the name given to a high-pressure system that stalls and blocks the normal eastward progression of weather systems.

The current high first drifted into the Tasman Sea back on Monday, and by Friday was still just east of Bass Strait, a position modelling expects will hold for at least another week.

And the stubborn high has completely jammed up Australia's weather chart, both deflecting cold fronts and lows well south of eastern states, while also ensuring winds are blowing in the same direction at a similar speed every day.

Loading...

While most blocks only last a few days, the current stagnation may last up to a fortnight, removing the standard day-to-day variability typically experienced in mid-latitude climates.

The exact type of repetitive weather currently being experienced depends on your location in Australia in proximity to the high.

Showery east coast, days of sunshine for inland and south

Winds blow anticlockwise around highs in the Southern Hemisphere, so for areas north of the centre, an easterly airstream is dominant, and for the east coast north of about Sydney, that means onshore winds and a daily dose of showers.

Brisbane's forecast is comically consistent with showers and 25C or 26C every day until at least next weekend.

The persistent stream of moist onshore winds could even deliver more than 100 millimetres of rain near the New South Wales-Queensland border by next weekend.

However, the eastern inland will see little if any rain, since low pressure is usually required for significant precipitation for regions away from the coast.

West of the high, the anticlockwise rotation of winds is resulting in a northerly airstream, and that is an offshore direction for the southern coastline, explaining the unseasonably lengthy run of sunny days in Victoria and South Australia.

And if a difference of 1C in a week is too inconsistent, parts of the inland have the exact same temperatures forecast every day, a forecast so rare you would think it is a BOM glitch.

Bendigo is a prime example. The city is tipped to hit 25C with mostly sunshine until next Saturday, and that follows near identical highs ranging from 23C to 25C already this week.

You will not need to check the weather forecast in Bendigo for another week. (ABC News)

Dubbo is another location with an identical looking forecast: sunny and 27C for seven days straight.

Further west, Western Australia is far enough away from the Tasman high to see regular cold fronts, so Perth's forecast during the coming week is far more changeable than eastern capitals.

Jet stream anchors high-pressure system in Tasman Sea

So why is a high-pressure system stuck in the Tasman when the Earth is still spinning？

Blocking patterns at the surface are associated with abnormal behaviour of jet streams about 10 kilometres above the ground.

Jets are fast flowing ribbons of wind that both blow from west to east and can travel at speeds well above 200 kilometres per hour.

There are two jet streams in each hemisphere — the subtropical and the polar — and under normal conditions they are close enough to keep weather systems mobile in the mid-latitudes.

The subtropical jet stream typically sits at a latitude of about 25 to 30 south, stretching from about WA's Central West to south-east Queensland.

But the jet is currently bending well north over Queensland, reaching a tropical latitude in the Coral Sea equal to Cairns.

A split in the polar and sub-tropical jet streams over eastern Australia is cradling a stationary high-pressure system. (ABC News)

In the meantime, the polar jet is diving south below New Zealand, and that has opened up a broad region of calm winds, the perfect environment for the cradling of a strong high in the Tasman Sea.

However, the relationship between highs and jets is complex.

Once a strong high has stalled, it helps to divert the very jet stream that split to cause the high's formation.

With both systems now reinforcing each other, blocks have the potential to last for several weeks.

Thankfully, the current blocking high will not bring severe weather, but Tasman blocks can produce flooding along the eastern seaboard, and in summer can prolong heatwaves over south-east Australia for weeks.

Eventually a blocking pattern will weaken, and at this stage the weather charts are likely to unlock and remobilise when a stronger front approaches south-east Australia.

However, according to some modelling, that may not occur until after next weekend.

World.title: Indigenous solar projects to tackle diesel shortage concerns and halve power bills
World.content:
Two remote Northern Territory Indigenous communities have attracted a combined $11 million in federal government funding for solutions to help tackle their fuel security and cost-of-living crises.

Borroloola in the Gulf of Carpentaria and Santa Teresa in Central Australia have secured $8 million and $3 million, respectively, towards building their own solar farms and micro grids, which will enable them to supply most of their own communities' electricity needs.

One of the developers of the Borroloola project, community leader Scott McDinny, said because it would not rely on expensive diesel and all the profits would be returned to the community, the project would reduce all Borroloola residents' power bills by 50 per cent.

"The solar system will reduce the cost of power, so everyone will have more money to go towards food," he said.

Scott McDinny says the project will reduce power bills for the community. (Supplied: Rebecca Parker )

Borroloola Garawa community leader Gadrian Hoosan said the project was much needed because the community's 750 residents were struggling to afford power cards to keep their electricity on more than ever, as the global fuel crisis pushed diesel and food prices higher.

He said the community could not wait for the cheaper power being promised from the 2.1 megawatt solar farm and 1.8 megawatt battery.

"Everybody in the community is excited about it," he said.

Gadrian Hoosan hopes the community's energy security and affordability will be improved by the project. (ABC News: Jane Bardon )

"It means a lot because our diesel costs are too high, and our power [costs] are too high.

" The renewable energy will make it a lot easier for a lot of the people in our community. "

Solar farm construction to begin next year

The Borroloola project is being developed by an Indigenous corporation called Original Power, in partnership with a new company in the community called Ngardara.

Mr McDinny, who chairs Ngardara, said the partners had received good indications they would be able to raise the rest of the $19 million they needed to fund the project, which would allow them to start building the solar farm by the beginning of 2027.

"We think other communities will be looking at us and we'll be able to share what we've done, and hopefully we can lower the cost of living," he said.

Loading...

Borroloola is one of hundreds of remote communities that are worried that global fuel shortages will stop them getting diesel for their local power stations.

Mr McDinny said once built, the Borroloola solar project would provide 80 per cent of the community's power, while residents would still rely on the NT government's local power station for the remaining 20 per cent.

But he said the project would reduce the station's diesel needs by 1.2 million litres each year.

"We are like 380 kilometres east from the Stuart Highway, so it's hard to get the diesel out here, and it costs the government a whole lot of money to get the diesel out here, so we're trying to reduce the cost of bringing diesel out here," Mr McDinny said.

The Ngardara Company and Original Power say the federal money will enable them to start building their project early next year. (ABC News: Rebecca Parker )

Strict conditions on connecting to grid

Original Power co-director Madie Sturgess said the Borroloola project had been planned for six years.

She said the biggest hurdle had been getting permission to connect to the Northern Territory government-owned grid.

Rewiring the planet Countries across the globe are racing to rewire their electricity systems for a decarbonised future. In Australia, delays are mounting, along with doubts about whether it can meet goals on schedule.

"Anyone who is trying to put up a renewable project in this country knows how hard it is, challenging the utilities to engage with the energy transition," Ms Sturgess said.

"We are seeing development delays across the country because of this, but we've taken an approach of being deeply collaborative with the utilities so that we can co-design a process that will work for everyone.

" We're hoping that we've set a precedent that makes it easier for anyone that comes after us. "

Hopes for reduced power prices in Santa Teresa

The other project in Santa Teresa has received $3 million in federal funding.

NT community builds first Indigenous-owned solar microgrid An Indigenous-owned solar farm, the first to be connected to a power grid, has been opened.

One of its developers, community leader Matthew Cavanagh, is also hoping that the project will reduce electricity prices in his community.

"We've got a problem with the power," he said.

"We go to the store and buy power cards, and it costs too much money.

"People get frustrated and upset asking, 'How come the power cards run out real quick?'"

Matthew Cavanagh says his community is fed up with expensive power. (ABC News: Jane Bardon )

The Santa Teresa and Borroloola projects have been funded through the federal government's $125 million Regional Microgrids Program.

The government has previously awarded money from the fund to projects in South Australia and Western Australia.

But Nick Dorward, from federal government renewable energy agency ARENA, said the two Northern Territory projects were special because they were the first fully Indigenous-owned projects to receive funding.

"This is about getting First Nations communities off dirty diesel and getting reliable energy, but extra important is the fact that these two projects are actually owned, developed and delivered by the communities themselves," he said.

Indigenous Australians Minister Malarndirri McCarthy said she hoped other communities would be able to replicate the projects to improve their energy security.

Malarndirri McCarthy says she would like to see other Indigenous communities establish similar projects. (Supplied: Rebecca Parker )

"We see what's happening around the world at the moment in terms of energy, and what we're seeing here today is two communities really stepping up and saying 'we want to have a future in this space', and our government is supporting that," she said.

World.content:
NationalWAAnzac Day ‘Cretins’: WA’s Anzac Day dawn service hecklers called out for ‘disgraceful’ behaviour Holly Thompson April 25, 2026 — 10:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

West Australian ministers and RSL WA members have called out the “disgusting and disrespectful acts” of a small group, who attended the state’s Anzac Day dawn service on Saturday morning and yelled out during the proceedings. The hecklers called out as Di Ryder, army veteran and Noongar elder, read out the Welcome to Country. The premier labelled the hecklers as “disgusting and disrespectful”. Holly Thompson RSL WA chief executive Stephen Barton, who was emceeing the event, stood up after the disruption and called the behaviour “one of the most disgraceful things I’ve ever heard”. His statement was met by applause from the crowd.



“To the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, we will continue to acknowledge country, we will not be bullied,” he said. At a press conference after the service, WA Premier Roger Cook took the opportunity to also call out the “disgusting and disrespectful acts of a very small number of people”. “Anzac Day is a day that we come together. We come together as a sense of unity and with a sense of strength and resilience,” he said. “For anyone to disrespect one of our elders and a former veteran themselves is just disgusting and disrespectful.” RSL WA state president Duncan Anderson said they were “cretins”.



“[They] are entitled to their own views. Ironically, that’s what we serve for to uphold the freedom of speech and democracy,” he said. “But everyone just needs to realise that Anzac Day, particularly the dawn service, is a politics-free zone. Di Ryder after finishing her speech. Colin Murty “It’s about commemorating those who have sacrificed and served, and people just need to shelve their opinions for a couple of minutes and just behave themselves.” He said Di Ryder was a friend and that she had shown courage by continuing her speech and ignoring the calls, labelling the support of the crowd as heartwarming.



“Di Ryder is a proud veteran, and not only did they disrespect her heritage, they disrespected the fact that she’s a veteran, and that’s disgusting on Anzac Day,” Anderson said. Defence Industries and Veterans Minister Paul Papalia has announced the launch of two new programs to support WA veterans. The state government has committed $400,000 to fund 80 veteran-focused scholarships over next four years, to help veterans upskill and prepare for employment opportunities in WA’s defence industry. World.title: Loud boos mar Anzac Day dawn services in Martin Place and Melbourne
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWAnzac Day Loud boos mar Anzac Day dawn services in Martin Place and Melbourne Patrick Begley, Jack Gramenz and Sally Rawsthorne Updated April 25, 2026 — 10:39am ,first published April 24, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Save this article for later Add articles to your saved list and come back to them anytime. Got it Share A A A

Two hours before the sun rose, they stood gathered in uniforms, blazers and hoodies to remember the fallen. Thousands of people attended the ANZAC Day dawn service at the Martin Place Cenotaph in Sydney, a camera drone winking above them, as wreaths were laid, hymns sung and tears shed. “It’s much bigger than I thought,” said John Murray, 89, a Vietnam veteran who made the trip from Brisbane to see what he believed was the biggest dawn service in Australia. The son of a Rat of Tobruk, Murray wore a blue RAAF cap and a row of medals pinned to his coat, including a British Empire Medal for his services in medical evacuation. Loading “They do it very well here,” he said of the ceremony. The minute of silence was solemn, unbroken. But earlier, a number of crowd members booed loudly and repeatedly during an Acknowledgment of Country by Uncle Ray Minniecon.



Minniecon, whose grandfather served with the Light Horse Brigade, continued despite the interruption and was applauded when he finished. “We have experienced this type of racism for over 200 years,” he told media after the service. “One of the questions that we have in our minds is: What crime did we commit to attract this kind of racism?” Vietnam Veteran, 89-year-old John Murray at the ANZAC day dawn service in Martin Place, Sydney. Louise Kennerley NSW Police in a statement said officers responded to an alleged act of nuisance and arrested a 24-year-old man. Booing also marred the Welcome to Country ahead of the service at Melbourne’s Shrine of Remembrance. A small group of men booed again when Victorian Governor Margaret Gardner acknowledged the Bunurong people of the eastern Kulin nation at the start of her speech.



Last year, a Welcome to Country during a dawn service in Melbourne was booed by members of the neo-Nazi National Socialist Network. Uncle Ray Minniecon whose Acknowledgment of Country was interrupted by loud booing. Louise Kennerley Official reaction has been fast and furious. Defence Minister Richard Marles branded the booing “deeply disappointing”. “Acknowledgements of Country are just an act of respect – and what characterises today is, it is a day of respect,” Marles told ABC TV. Premier Chris Minns said he was disappointed by the actions of a small number of people.



“Whist I’ve never before heard booing like that at a dawn service, I’ve also never heard a crowd spontaneously applaud as they did for Uncle Ray Minniecon,” Minns said. Victorian Premier Jacinta Allen said that booing “disrespects everyone who fought and died for our freedom”. “Politicising this sacred day is bastardy. I condemn it and so should every leader,” she said. On Saturday morning, the organiser for the anti-immigration March for Australia movement, Bec Freedom, posted on Telegram “Sydney boo’d”, followed by a salute emoji. March for Australia is closely linked to the National Socialist Network, which claims to have disbanded to avoid being proscribed as a hate group.



Emile Tauati, a warrant officer in the navy, said everyone was entitled to their opinion but “I do believe there’s a time and a place”. Tauati woke at 2am to attend the “very moving” service, his first in his hometown of Sydney after 16 years of military service. In previous years he was away, on base or at sea. Premier Chris Minns read the poem Salute by Sydney Elliott Napier, an annual tradition at the service. Other notable attendees included opposition leader Kellie Sloane, federal Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek, Governor Margaret Beazley and acting head of the RSL, Brigadier Vincent Williams (retired). Paul Simpfendorfer, a warrant officer in the army who most recently deployed to South Sudan, said he was up before dawn to “remember people I’ve served with.” Some had lost their lives in operations, others in training. “For me, it’s paying respect to my forbears,” Simpfendorfer said.



The service in Martin Place, Sydney, began at 4.20am. Louise Kennerley The dawn service at the Cenotaph in Martin Place. Louise Kennerley Stacey Nicholson with son two-year old son Bodhi woke early to attend the service at Martin Place. Louise Kennerley Stacey Nicholson, whose uncle served in the military, attended her first service with her partner and two-year-old son Bodhi, who sucked on a pacifier while toying with a commemorative sprig of rosemary. “I think it’s always important to honour our history,” Nicholson said. “We are very, very lucky in the life we have.”



Thousands of people are expected to pay tribute to Australia’s veteran community at Anzac Day ceremonies and events across NSW and around Australia this long weekend. Where to commemorate Anzac Day in Sydney? The major official commemorations are taking place at the Martin Place Cenotaph and near the Anzac Memorial in Hyde Park. Dawn at Bondi Beach. Janie Barrett WWII veteran, 99-year-old Roy Pearsonat, at the start of the Anzac Day march in Sydney. Louise Kennerley



Vietnam veteran Rod White, a former RSL president, gets ready to march. Louise Kennerley NSW will have a public holiday on Monday, April 27, as April 25 falls on a weekend this year. The Monday public holiday is part of a two-year trial that will also capture Anzac Day falling on a Sunday in 2027. The dawn service is followed by a march along Elizabeth Street at 9am, before a commemoration service at the Pool of Remembrance, near the Anzac Memorial in Hyde Park at 12.30pm. A sunset service will take place at the Martin Place Cenotaph at 5pm. Related Article Updated

Anzac Day Roberts-Smith attends Anzac Day dawn service on the Gold Coast



Other community events are being held around the state by RSL sub-branches. In Parramatta, a march gathered at the town hall at 4am, proceeding to Prince Alfred Square before a dawn service at 4.30am. In Penrith, the dawn service assembled outside the Penrith RSL club before a silent march to Memory Park. The RSL club will be providing a breakfast following the service. A Newcastle dawn service commenced at 5am at Camp Shortland on Nobbys Beach, before a march from Perkins Street to Civic Park at 9.15am and a commemoration service at Civic Park Cenotaph at 10am, featuring an RAAF flyover. A Wollongong dawn service, also at 5am, was held at the MacCabe Park Cenotaph on Church Street, followed by a march on Crown Street at 10am.



How to get around the city on Anzac Day Anzac Day at Coogee. Audrey Richardson Major road closures are in place throughout the day and public transport is encouraged. Travel is free for veterans, currently serving ADF personnel, and their families. Eligibility applies for people in uniform, wearing their medals or with proof of military service. Additional services are running to Martin Place, but light rail services did not run between Town Hall and Circular Quay until 6.15am, and will pause again between 12.30pm and 1.30pm. Buses through the city may take different routes and stops. Related Article Perspective

Anzac Day ‘He died at the moment the war ended’: The young Australian who helped the Czech partisans



What’s open and closed on Anzac Day? Anzac Day is a restricted trading day. Major retailers, including supermarkets and department stores, will be closed all day. Small shops, chemists, newsagencies, service stations, cafes, takeaway food outlets and licensed venues can open. The public holiday on Monday is not a restricted trading day. Where can I play two-up?



Chances are if a pub is open on Anzac Day you’ll be able to play two-up there. It’s one of the three days of the year the game, played by World War One Diggers, is allowed. Venues don’t need a permit but have to ensure the game is played in its traditional format. Liquor & Gaming NSW inspectors will be checking. Are double demerits in effect? Yes. Double demerits are already in force and will continue throughout the weekend, including Monday. Random breath testing and mobile drug testing will also be conducted across the state. You can expect an increased police presence on major highways and regional routes due to expected increases in traffic over the long weekend.

World.title: Air New Zealand plane in Auckland with mechanical issues forces flights to divert
World.content:
Photo: AFP

A mechanical issue on the Auckland Airport runway forced several flights to be diverted on Saturday morning.

Air New Zealand's chief risk and safety officer Nathan McGraw said the plane had a fault with its braking system.

"Flight NZ81 from Auckland to Hong Kong experienced a technical issue with the braking system when positioning for take-off at the end of the runway this morning.

"The aircraft is being towed from the runway where customers will disembark and the aircraft will be assessed by our engineers."

A witness told 1News smoke had appeared as the aircraft was taxiing before taking off.

The fault caused several arriving international flights to temporarily divert into a holding pattern while the runway was cleared.

A spokesperson said operations are now returning to normal.

Flights are now landing, but some have had their arrivals delayed by over 30 minutes.

McGraw said customers would be reaccommodated on an alternative aircraft.

World.title: Live: Anzac Day commemorations around New Zealand
World.content:
New Zealanders at home and around the world will gather to mark Anzac Day in recognition of the first big military action by Australian and New Zealand soldiers in Gallipoli in 1915.

From dawn services to parades and ceremonies at RSAs, people across the country will gather to reflect on the atrocities of war, remember those who died, and honour the contributions of returned service personnel.

The theme for this year's Anzac commemoration is 'Pasifika' - acknowledging the contribution of island soldiers from across the region.

Follow the latest from today's commemorations in the live blog above.
